newsitem.title: USA: U.S FX pros glum as execs predict further shakeout.
newsitem.headline: U.S FX pros glum as execs predict further shakeout.

text.p: U.S. foreign exchange professionals are jittery after senior managers at two major dealing firms suggested industry downsizing will probably accelerate, according to industry sources.

The executives, David Puth, managing director at Chase Manhattan Bank, and Jamie Thorsen, senior vice president at Bank of Montreal, recently predicted the number of participants in the North American currency markets could shrink by more than half by the turn of the century.

"Dave Puth and I did this last year as well," said Thorsen, confirming her comments at a panel discussion on the issue. "When we talked about what we were going to do, I basically said I think it's important that we're honest with people so that they can be best prepared."
A videotape of the panel discussion, in which Puth and Thorsen participated, was made available to Reuters. Puth did not return calls for further comment.
"Everybody is spooked. Brokers are really spooked and a lot of dealers are spooked," said John Barlow, a senior dealer from Bayerische Landesbank Girozentrale, who attended the recent session.
Both executives presided over mergers of large U.S. trading operations over the last year and lamented the toll of recent industry consolidation.
Puth told the audience he was certain the trend towards bank merging and broker merging would "absolutely" continue and probably at a "faster pace."

"I agree with David," Bank of Montreal's Thorsen said on the video. "There is a very strong possiblity that in five years, 50 percent of the people sitting in this room may or may not be in our particular line of business."
The advent of electronic currency broking has already taken a stiff toll on live telephone or "voice" brokers.

The electronic age has also nearly eliminated the profitable edge trading firms possess when quoting to customers by making the indicative prices available to them on screens more reflective of the actual market between banks, experts attending the conference said.

If the market gets to the point were there is total "clarity" of price on traders' screens, the foreign exchange market could go the way of the U.S. government bond market, where there are five or six people who make meaningful money, Thorsen and Puth agreed.
"It's kind of interesting to hear those senior people be so blunt," said David Gilmore, partner at consulting firm Foreign Exchange Analytics, who was present at the forum.
At the same time, information technology has jacked up the costs of running a large dealing room while enabling better-informed customers to demand ever narrower bid/offer spreads from trading firms.
The firms have in turn seen profit margins on trading and customer business evaporate, the managers said.

The recent shakeout in the U.S. forex industry, particularly the departure of HSBC Holdings Plc unit HSBC Midland from the U.S. interbank foreign exchange market, provided a gloomy backdrop for the conference.

HSBC Midland -- one of the largest banks in the world and regarded as having one of the market's premier foreign exchange operations -- eliminated 55 U.S. positions in trading, operations and finance earlier this month in a move to centralize out of London.

As market volatility decreases and Europe moves towards implementing a single currency, banks will have to change the way they manage currency risk and should put resources into providing "value-added" services, Puth told the conference.
Remaining competitive will depend on a bank's ability to provide services like economic research, solid settlement operations and exotic currency capabilities, he said.

"I wouldn't be surprised if ... there will be a handful of niche participants, and everybody else will decide -- with the costs involved and consequences of things like (a) single (European) currency -- the operational hassles of dealing with exotic currencies and limited client presence are probably not worth the investment," Puth said on the video.
